title: What is GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux) — Git as the single source of truth with a controller continuously reconciling the cluster to the declared manifests (pull-based) — and how does it differ from a push-based Jenkins deploy (auditability, automatic drift correction, easy rollback via `git revert`)?

s1_definition.profdef: GitOps is an operational model where a Git repository holds the complete declared desired state of a system as manifests, and a controller running inside the cluster, such as ArgoCD or Flux, continuously compares the live cluster to that Git state and reconciles any difference by pulling and applying the manifests. It is pull-based: the cluster converges itself toward Git rather than an external tool pushing changes in. A push-based Jenkins deploy is the opposite: a pipeline from outside the cluster runs commands like `kubectl apply` to imperatively push a change into the cluster. GitOps gives stronger auditability (every change is a reviewed Git commit), automatic drift correction (the controller undoes any out-of-band change), and trivial rollback (a `git revert` restores the previous declared state).
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India's official rulebook for how every branch must be set up. In GitOps, the rulebook lives in a locked, version-controlled master binder (Git), and each branch has an inspector (the controller) who constantly walks the floor comparing reality to the rulebook and silently fixing anything that drifted — a moved desk, an unauthorised sign. To change a branch, you do not touch the branch directly; you amend the master binder through a reviewed change, and the inspector makes reality match. The old push model is like head office sending a courier who physically rearranges the branch; if someone later moves a desk, nobody notices, and to undo a change you need another courier trip. GitOps makes the binder the single truth and the inspector keep reality honest.
s1_definition.oneliner: GitOps makes Git the single source of truth and an in-cluster controller continuously pulls reality toward it, so you get audit, automatic drift correction, and rollback by git revert — unlike a push-based Jenkins kubectl apply.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** GitOps is an operational model where a Git repository holds the complete declared desired state of a system as manifests, and a controller running inside the cluster, such as ArgoCD or Flux, continuously compares the live cluster to that Git state and reconciles any difference by pulling and applying the manifests. It is pull-based: the cluster converges itself toward Git rather than an external tool pushing changes in. A push-based Jenkins deploy is the opposite: a pipeline from outside the cluster runs commands like `kubectl apply` to imperatively push a change into the cluster. GitOps gives stronger auditability (every change is a reviewed Git commit), automatic drift correction (the controller undoes any out-of-band change), and trivial rollback (a `git revert` restores the previous declared state).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India's official rulebook for how every branch must be set up. In GitOps, the rulebook lives in a locked, version-controlled master binder (Git), and each branch has an inspector (the controller) who constantly walks the floor comparing reality to the rulebook and silently fixing anything that drifted — a moved desk, an unauthorised sign. To change a branch, you do not touch the branch directly; you amend the master binder through a reviewed change, and the inspector makes reality match. The old push model is like head office sending a courier who physically rearranges the branch; if someone later moves a desk, nobody notices, and to undo a change you need another courier trip. GitOps makes the binder the single truth and the inspector keep reality honest.

**One line to remember:** GitOps makes Git the single source of truth and an in-cluster controller continuously pulls reality toward it, so you get audit, automatic drift correction, and rollback by git revert — unlike a push-based Jenkins kubectl apply.

sections.s2_technical:
In GitOps the desired state is declarative and lives in Git. For a banking service this is a set of Kubernetes manifests, usually Helm charts or Kustomize overlays, describing the Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, and the exact image tag. There is typically a separate config repository per environment or an overlay per environment, so the Prod folder declares exactly what should run in Prod.

The controller runs inside the cluster and watches both Git and the live cluster. ArgoCD, for example, defines an `Application` resource pointing at a Git repo path and a target namespace. It periodically (and on webhook) fetches the manifests, computes a diff against the live objects, and if they differ it is "OutOfSync." Depending on policy it either shows the drift for a human to sync or, with automated sync enabled, applies the manifests itself to make the cluster match Git.

Drift correction is a core behaviour. If someone runs a manual `kubectl edit` to bump replicas in Prod, the controller detects that the live state no longer matches Git and, with self-heal enabled, reverts it back to what Git declares. This is impossible in a pure push model, where an out-of-band change simply persists unnoticed until it causes an incident.

Deployment in GitOps is a Git commit, not a kubectl command. The CI pipeline still builds and tests and produces an image tag, but instead of deploying, it opens a pull request (or commits) to the config repo updating the image tag for the target environment. Once that commit is merged, the controller notices and rolls it out. So the pipeline's job ends at "propose the desired state," and the controller owns "make it real."

Rollback becomes `git revert`. Because the cluster always reflects Git, reverting the commit that bumped the image tag causes the controller to roll the cluster back to the previous tag automatically. There is no separate rollback script and no risk of the rollback itself drifting, because Git remains the single truth.

Contrast with push-based Jenkins. There, Jenkins holds cluster credentials and runs `kubectl apply` or `helm upgrade` directly. The downsides are concrete: the record of what is actually deployed lives in Jenkins build logs rather than a reviewable Git history; any manual change to the cluster is invisible and permanent; rollback means re-running an old pipeline or a manual command; and Jenkins must store powerful cluster credentials, widening the attack surface.

A senior nuance is the security boundary. In GitOps the cluster credentials never leave the cluster, because the controller pulls from Git using read-only repo access, so an external CI breach cannot directly touch the cluster. Another nuance is that CI and CD are cleanly separated: CI produces artifacts and proposes state, the controller applies it. A third nuance is the "app of apps" or environment-promotion pattern, where promoting from QA to Prod is literally a commit copying a tested image tag from the QA overlay to the Prod overlay, which keeps promotion auditable and reversible.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India an engineer ran a manual kubectl command at 2 a.m. during an incident to bump the transfer service replicas, and forgot to put it back. Weeks later a deploy reset it and capacity silently dropped, causing a slowdown during peak hours. Nobody could tell what the cluster was supposed to look like. This is exactly the problem GitOps drift correction solves. The desired state lives in Git, and the controller would have flagged or reverted the manual change immediately so reality always matches the reviewed truth.

Problem 2 — A rollback of a bad fee change required an engineer to find and re-run an old Jenkins job, and under pressure they picked the wrong build number and made it worse. This is exactly the problem GitOps rollback solves. Reverting the Git commit that changed the image tag restores the exact previous declared state, and the controller rolls it back automatically.

Problem 3 — An auditor asked "what exactly is running in Prod right now and who approved it?" and the only answer was scattered Jenkins logs. This is exactly the problem GitOps auditability solves. The Prod folder in Git, plus its commit history and pull-request approvals, is a complete, reviewable record.

To make this concrete without a real cluster we will write a Java simulation. We will model a `GitRepo` holding the desired image tag (the source of truth), a `Cluster` holding the live image tag, and a `GitOpsController` that periodically reconciles the cluster toward Git, with self-heal that reverts drift. We will also model a `PushDeployer` representing the old Jenkins style for contrast. We will deploy via a Git commit and watch the controller apply it, simulate a manual drift and watch the controller heal it, then perform a `git revert` and watch the controller roll back. This mirrors the real pull-based reconciliation loop.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run it
java -cp target/classes com.bank.gitops.GitOpsDemo

# Real usage: install ArgoCD and register the Application, then deploy by commit:
# git commit -am "bump transfer-service to 1.1.0" && git push
# Rollback:
# git revert <sha> && git push     # ArgoCD rolls the cluster back automatically
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is an initial state where both Git and the cluster run `transfer-service:1.0.0`, followed by a deploy, a manual drift, a rollback, and a push-style deploy.

Step 1: CI proposes a new desired state by committing `transfer-service:1.1.0` to Git. At this moment Git says 1.1.0 but the cluster still runs 1.0.0, so they are out of sync.

Step 2: The controller reconciles. It compares desired (1.1.0) to live (1.0.0), finds them different, and because self-heal is on it applies 1.1.0 to the cluster. Now both match and the state is SYNCED.

Step 3: Someone runs a manual kubectl change, overriding the live cluster to `hotfix-manual`. Git still says 1.1.0, so the cluster has drifted away from the truth.

Step 4: The controller reconciles again. It sees the live tag no longer matches Git, flags OUT_OF_SYNC, and self-heals by reapplying 1.1.0, erasing the unauthorised manual change automatically.

Step 5: A rollback is needed, so an engineer does a git revert, popping the history back to 1.0.0. Git now declares 1.0.0 while the cluster runs 1.1.0.

Step 6: The controller reconciles and rolls the cluster back to 1.0.0 to match Git, with no rollback script needed. Finally, a push-style Jenkins deploy sets the live cluster to an untracked tag, but because Git still says 1.0.0, the very next reconcile heals it back, showing that in a GitOps world the controller, not an external push, has the final word.

```
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] === Deploy via Git commit ===
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [WARNING] OUT_OF_SYNC: live=transfer-service:1.0.0 desired=transfer-service:1.1.0 -> healing
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] RECONCILED: cluster now runs transfer-service:1.1.0
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] === Drift: someone runs manual kubectl ===
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [WARNING] OUT_OF_SYNC: live=transfer-service:hotfix-manual desired=transfer-service:1.1.0 -> healing
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] RECONCILED: cluster now runs transfer-service:1.1.0
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] === Rollback via git revert ===
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [WARNING] OUT_OF_SYNC: live=transfer-service:1.1.0 desired=transfer-service:1.0.0 -> healing
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] RECONCILED: cluster now runs transfer-service:1.0.0
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] === Contrast: old push-based Jenkins deploy ===
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] Jenkins kubectl apply -> transfer-service:1.2.0-untracked (no drift tracking)
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [WARNING] OUT_OF_SYNC: live=transfer-service:1.2.0-untracked desired=transfer-service:1.0.0 -> healing
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] RECONCILED: cluster now runs transfer-service:1.0.0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  CI builds image:1.1.0
    │ (does NOT deploy)
    ▼
  commit to Config Repo (Git = source of truth)
    │
    ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  GitOps Controller (ArgoCD)   │  ← runs INSIDE cluster, pulls Git
  │  loop: desired vs live        │
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ diff?
        ┌────────┴─────────┐
        ▼ in sync          ▼ out of sync
     do nothing       apply desired → Cluster

  Drift path:
    manual kubectl edit → live != Git → controller self-heals → live == Git

  Rollback path:
    git revert → Git = previous tag → controller applies → cluster rolls back

  Push (old): Jenkins kubectl apply → live changes, but next reconcile heals to Git
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
GitOps is an operational model where a Git repository holds the complete declared desired state of the system as manifests, and a controller running inside the cluster, such as ArgoCD or Flux, continuously compares the live cluster to that Git state and reconciles any difference. It is pull-based: the cluster converges itself toward Git rather than an outside tool pushing changes in. Deploying is no longer a kubectl command; it is a reviewed Git commit that updates the image tag, and the controller notices and rolls it out.

The differences from a push-based Jenkins deploy are concrete. Auditability is far stronger, because what is running is exactly what the Git history and its pull-request approvals say, rather than something buried in Jenkins build logs. Drift is corrected automatically, because if someone makes a manual change in the cluster the controller detects that the live state no longer matches Git and, with self-heal enabled, reverts it. Rollback is trivial, because reverting the commit that changed the image tag makes the controller roll the cluster back to the previous declared state, with no rollback script and no chance of the rollback itself drifting.

The security story is a major reason banks adopt it. In GitOps the cluster credentials never leave the cluster; the controller pulls from Git with read-only access, so a breach of the external CI system cannot directly touch the cluster. CI and CD are cleanly separated: CI builds and tests the artifact and proposes the new desired state, and the in-cluster controller owns actually applying it.

On the banking project we moved the transfer service from Jenkins running kubectl apply to ArgoCD watching a config repo. Deploys became commits that bumped the image tag in the Prod overlay, promotion from QA to Prod was a commit copying a tested tag between overlays, and rollback during an incident was a single git revert that ArgoCD applied automatically. The incident that originally motivated this was a 2 a.m. manual kubectl change that silently drifted and later caused a slowdown; with self-heal on, the controller would have reverted that drift within the next reconcile. The senior point I always add is that this eliminates the "what is actually running and who approved it" problem that auditors always ask about, because Git is the single, reviewable source of truth and the controller keeps reality honest.
